item.text: {"chapter_id":"8B","judge_orientation":"Retain a balanced, passage-supported portfolio showing a clear but internally shifting program, substantial resource and institutional mobilization, mixed social and economic delivery, serious security and health implementation gaps, limited demonstrated adaptation, and unresolved attribution between presidential direction, agencies, subnational actors, inherited conditions, external shocks, and joint programs. Do not score from this list alone; reopen the full ledger before judging.","entries":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0048-E014","reason_to_read":"Establishes the administration’s contemporaneous declared portfolio across poverty, social programs, wages, public goods, environmental policy, climate adaptation, and multilateral goals.","role":"context","supported_lenses":["8B.1"],"corrected_summary":"Mexico’s September 2023 UN statement presented the government’s declared priorities, including poverty reduction, social programs, minimum-wage increases, public goods and infrastructure, environmental sustainability, climate adaptation, and treaty-based multilateralism; it establishes stated goals but not implementation or outcomes."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E001","reason_to_read":"Provides the more discriminating baseline for security: pacification through social causes, employment, welfare, reconciliation, and reduced military deployment, followed by creation of a military-rooted National Guard and erosion of the withdrawal expectation.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.6","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"Mexico Evalúa reports that López Obrador campaigned and initially framed pacification around social causes and reduced reliance on military deployment, but his 2018–2024 plan created a military-rooted National Guard and the expectation of withdrawing the armed forces from the streets soon diminished."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0044-E011","reason_to_read":"Shows formal operationalization of a security program through mandatory federal application, assigned ministry monitoring, oversight, and budget-funded implementation, while not proving execution.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"The 2022–2024 National Public Security Program formally established multidimensional and rights-oriented objectives, made them mandatory for federal agencies, assigned monitoring and oversight to specified ministries, and required implementation through approved budgets; the passage does not show whether those arrangements achieved results."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E001","reason_to_read":"Documents 2023 prioritization and resource allocation across social programs, including large increases for adult pensions and fertilizers and reductions for emergency support and health and medicines.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL reports that the 16 priority programs received 512,805 million pesos in 2023, with uneven changes from 2020: large increases for Fertilizers and the older-adult pension, but reductions for emergency assistance and the health-and-medicines program; this establishes budget priorities, not service quality or personal presidential control."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E002","reason_to_read":"Direct 2023 evidence that three of sixteen priority programs had unclear target populations and that the health program’s stated purpose was reduced to transferring resources rather than specifying a population and intended result.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"In 2023, CONEVAL found that 13 of 16 priority programs identified their target population adequately, while three did not; the health-and-medicines program specified only transfers to states, without clearly identifying its target population or intended change."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E004","reason_to_read":"Directly tests monitoring and adaptation: four programs representing nearly 20% of the priority-program budget were classified as Management and did not measure results, while monitoring recommendations had been disregarded to varying degrees.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.6","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL classified four 2023 priority programs as Management because their central objectives did not clearly identify the public problem; together they represented nearly 20% of the priority-program budget and did not measure results. The report also states that monitoring recommendations had been disregarded to varying degrees, without identifying personal presidential direction."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E005","reason_to_read":"Shows incomplete coverage instrumentation and mixed target attainment, with ten of fourteen programs exceeding planned absolute coverage but four falling short and two lacking coverage indicators.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"For 2023 monitoring, only 14 of 16 priority programs had coverage indicators; using definitive 2022 data, ten exceeded planned absolute coverage and four fell short, while Sembrando Vida and the health-and-medicines program had no coverage indicator. Coverage does not establish quality or welfare improvement."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0048-E009","reason_to_read":"Provides a concrete mixed process-evaluation record: operational rules, updated registries, technical coordination, and local problem-solving coexisted with supply shortages, distribution and banking bottlenecks, weak planning, and insufficient outcome indicators.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL found that Sembrando Vida had defined beneficiary rules, monthly registry updates, technical accompaniment, and local coordination practices, but also supply and distribution shortages, banking bottlenecks, planning problems, and insufficient indicators for monitoring social and food-sufficiency outcomes."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0032-E003","reason_to_read":"Supplies the strongest health-transition chain: the 2018–2022 access deprivation increase coincided with the Seguro Popular–Insabi transition, coordination problems, lower proportional health spending, and greater out-of-pocket burdens, with attribution explicitly qualified.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL reports that health-access deprivation rose from 16.2% in 2018 to 39.1% in 2022 and associates the change with the Seguro Popular–Insabi transition, inadequate coordination, lower proportional health spending, pandemic effects, and Insabi limitations; it describes associations rather than a complete causal finding."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0032-E010","reason_to_read":"Shows observable service substitution and cost effects: public-sector care fell, private care increased, and catastrophic health spending remained above 2018 levels, while nearly all people seeking care received some care.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"Between 2018 and 2022, people reporting care in public institutions fell while private care rose; catastrophic health spending increased from 2.1% to 2.9% of households nationally and reached 4.2% in rural areas. Nearly all people who sought care received it, so the passage concerns access channels and financial burden, not clinical quality."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0013-E006","reason_to_read":"Shows a late-2023 corrective response to medicine shortages while preserving uncertainty about delivery: the centralized warehouse and promised 24–48-hour distribution were launched without evidence yet of reliable nationwide performance.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"At the end of the period, López Obrador launched a centralized medicine warehouse intended to supply hospitals through armed-forces or Birmex delivery within 24–48 hours. AP reported substantial earlier unfilled-prescription problems and expert concerns about centralization, but the passage does not establish whether the warehouse delivered reliably."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E007","reason_to_read":"Documents executed security mobilization: military institutions received most security spending, civil spending and local transfers fell, and the National Guard expanded substantially while remaining largely military in composition.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"From 2019 to 2023, military security institutions received 72.2% of security-institution spending; military spending rose while civil spending and federal transfers to states and municipalities fell. The National Guard’s personnel increased, but the passage also reports that it did not reach its initial staffing target, was not fully civil, and had incomplete police certification."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E008","reason_to_read":"Tests whether security mobilization translated into preventive and justice practice: local institutions performed nearly all emergency responses and prosecutorial presentations, while several National Guard activity measures worsened.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.5","8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"For 2020–2023, local security institutions accounted for 98.5% of emergency calls and 99.2% of prosecutorial presentations, while the National Guard accounted for 1.5% and 0.8%; National Guard presentations fell and armed confrontations rose. These are performance proxies and do not alone establish causal effects on crime."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E009","reason_to_read":"Preserves mixed and measurement-sensitive security outcomes: some crime measures declined, but the 2022–2023 reversal and possible homicide classification problems limit attribution.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"Mexico Evalúa reports a 17.3% homicide reduction between its comparison points and a 12% fall in reported crime from 2018 to 2023, but crime rose 15.9% from 2022 to 2023 and the report warns that homicide reductions may coincide with undercounting or reclassification of other offenses."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E011","reason_to_read":"Provides comparative evidence against attributing homicide reductions to National Guard activity, while stating the analysis is subnational and does not prove uniform effects.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"A Mexico Evalúa comparative analysis of 32 states found that homicide reduction was not consistently associated with greater National Guard activity; in its controlled minimization, absence of National Guard operations was the configuration associated with homicide reduction. The finding challenges, but does not by itself conclusively disprove, federal causal contribution."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0055-E006","reason_to_read":"Shows formal execution and institutional resistance: the executive’s transfer of National Guard control to Defense was invalidated in relevant provisions, but the effects were deferred until January 2024.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The Supreme Court held invalid key provisions transferring National Guard operational, administrative, budgetary, command, and transitional control to Defense; the challenged decree originated in the López Obrador administration, but the invalidity effects were postponed until January 2024, so the ruling did not immediately reverse the arrangement during 2023."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0013-E003","reason_to_read":"Retain as a bounded crisis-management and adaptation record, not as proof of personal direction: the GIEI records investigative advances alongside obstruction, turnover, withdrawn warrants, withheld information, and continuing delays.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.4","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The 2023 GIEI report recognized significant investigative advances by Omar Gómez and his team but also described pressure and turnover, withdrawn arrest warrants, delayed proceedings, and military or naval withholding of information documented by the experts; it does not prove that López Obrador personally ordered each obstruction or correction."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0030-E004","reason_to_read":"Provides a direct project-delivery test: the Maya Train opened only partially, with delays, incomplete track, sharply higher projected costs, and uncertain operating-cost recovery acknowledged by the president.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"In December 2023, López Obrador inaugurated only a partly completed Maya Train section amid hours-long delays; only one side of the planned double track was finished, projected cost had risen substantially from the original estimate, and the president said operating-cost coverage could take three or four years."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0040-E008","reason_to_read":"Adds audit-based implementation and control evidence beyond opening-day reporting: large rights-of-way expenditures lacked substantiation, property advances lacked completed ownership documents, and transfer to the Sedena-controlled operator remained incomplete.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"An external audit of the 2023 public account reported more than 2.442 billion pesos in rights-of-way payments awaiting substantiation and more than 5.684 billion pesos in property advances lacking completed legal ownership documents; transfer of the project to the Sedena-controlled company was also incomplete. The passage does not establish López Obrador’s personal knowledge of each irregularity."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E013","reason_to_read":"Provides independent portfolio balance: successful USMCA negotiation and restrained pandemic spending coexist with expanded military influence, weak security results, centralization, and an insufficient nearshoring strategy.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"CSIS assessed López Obrador’s record as mixed: it credited successful USMCA negotiation and restrained pandemic spending that avoided a major fiscal crisis, while describing expanded military influence, deteriorating security, centralization, and an insufficiently defined nearshoring strategy."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E014","reason_to_read":"Tests economic program execution through a concrete mixed chain: oil-contract and refinery choices, failed electricity reform, legislative limits, and continuing energy uncertainty.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The administration halted new foreign oil contracts, audited earlier awards, committed heavily to Dos Bocas, and pursued stronger state control of electricity; the constitutional reform failed in Congress, while energy-policy disputes and uncertainty continued. The passage supports implementation and legislative limits, not a complete outcome assessment."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E014","reason_to_read":"Adds independent countervailing economic evidence: 3.2% 2023 growth and identified administration priorities, while preserving pandemic, U.S. recovery, nearshoring, productivity, investment, and regulatory alternatives.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"The World Bank identifies the administration’s priorities as universal transfers, flagship infrastructure, the National Guard, the Isthmus corridor, Dos Bocas, energy self-sufficiency, and labor reforms, and reports 3.2% 2023 growth; it also notes subdued potential growth and warns that pandemic recovery, U.S. recovery, nearshoring, inflation, and other factors complicate attribution."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E015","reason_to_read":"Provides a broad, independent implementation ledger with both failures and adaptations: only eight of 24 partnership indicators achieved, many off track, client-requested cancellations and restructurings, and policy shifts and turnover affecting continuity.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"The World Bank’s 2023 review found eight of 24 partnership objective indicators achieved, one partially achieved, five on track, and ten off track; it linked implementation to pandemic effects, policy shifts, institutional turnover, security obstacles, cancellations, and reduced investment lending, while also recording continuing policy lending, advisory support, and project restructuring."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0031-E016","reason_to_read":"Supplies independent near-period outcome evidence for the social portfolio, with poverty improvement alongside sharply increased health-access deprivation and explicit limits on causal attribution.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.7","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL’s 2022 measurement, published in 2023, recorded poverty at 36.3% versus 43.9% in 2020, while health-access deprivation rose from 28.2% to 39.1%; these are 2022 outcomes, not full-year 2023 results, and the source does not assign them exclusively to López Obrador’s policies."}],"changes_from_draft":["Added the more discriminating security baseline and formal 2022–2024 security-program evidence; the September 2023 UN statement is retained only as one program statement.","Added direct 2023 monitoring evidence on target populations, result orientation, coverage indicators, unmeasured programs, and disregarded monitoring recommendations.","Added the health-system transition, public/private care shift, catastrophic spending, and the late-period medicine-warehouse response with explicit uncertainty about delivery success.","Retained and narrowed security mobilization and outcome evidence, adding comparative National Guard evidence and preserving measurement and causal limitations.","Retained Ayotzinapa only as a bounded mixed record of advances, obstruction, turnover, and institutional resistance; removed any implication of personal presidential direction of each act.","Added Supreme Court legal-correction evidence with the January 2024 effective-date qualification.","Expanded the Maya Train evidence with audit findings on unsubstantiated expenditures, property documentation, and incomplete transfer.","Added independent countervailing evidence on USMCA, fiscal restraint, economic growth, social transfers, World Bank-supported outputs, and mixed partnership performance.","Corrected all near-period outcome language to distinguish 2022 measurements published or used in 2023 from direct full-year 2023 outcomes.","Narrowed attribution throughout to administration-level or program-level evidence where personal López Obrador control is not established."],"unresolved_gaps":["Direct evidence of López Obrador’s personal role in agency-level successes, failures, monitoring decisions, and subordinate abuses remains limited.","Several strongest social and health outcome figures are for 2022, while definitive full-year 2023 outcome data and durability evidence remain incomplete.","The evidence does not fully separate federal action from subnational implementation, joint World Bank/UN programs, remittances, wages, nearshoring, pandemic recovery, and other external causes.","Systematic evidence that audits or evaluations caused presidential course correction, personnel replacement, or resource reallocation remains weak.","The security record contains conflicting outcome measures and possible classification problems; the comparative National Guard analysis warrants methodological review before decisive use.","The dossier does not yet provide complete evidence for environmental, climate, international, anti-corruption, and other material components of the broader stated portfolio."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["The future judge should reopen the full ledger before judgment because this revised list remains selective and cannot establish portfolio breadth or a holistic chapter result by itself.","Reopen to test whether omitted economic, international, environmental, anti-corruption, wage, education, and infrastructure evidence changes the balance across material programs.","Reopen to compare official claims with independent outcomes, audits, evaluations, and contrary evidence, especially where favorable results may reflect external trends or joint implementation.","Reopen to resolve whether apparent adaptation was substantive correction or merely formal monitoring, rebranding, cancellation, or institutional reassignment.","Reopen to assess the temporal lag from 2022 outcomes and 2023 launches to durable end-of-period results, including the Maya Train, health transition, National Guard arrangement, and social programs.","Reopen to calibrate ruler attribution and constraints across security, health, social policy, infrastructure, energy, trade, and fiscal policy before any score or confidence range is assigned."]}
